properties.name: Trajan
properties.one_line: The 63-year-old emperor died here around 8-9 August, worn out and dropsical after abandoning the failed siege of Hatra; the news broke at Antioch on 11 August, the day this map is set.

properties.name: Hadrian
properties.one_line: The 41-year-old legate of Syria was acclaimed emperor by the legions at Antioch on 11 August, the exact day this map is frozen on.

properties.name: Plotina
properties.one_line: Trajan's widow stood at his deathbed at Selinus and, according to hostile later gossip, helped secure Hadrian's succession in the confused hours afterward.

properties.name: Matidia
properties.one_line: Trajan's niece traveled with the imperial party and was present when he died at Selinus, then accompanied his ashes back toward Rome.

properties.name: Vibia Sabina
properties.location_117: Antioch, Syria (probable location, traveling with Hadrian's household)
properties.one_line: Hadrian's wife, married to him since 100, became empress this year as part of a household that had been based with him in the eastern provinces.

properties.name: Publius Acilius Attianus
properties.one_line: Hadrian's former guardian and joint praetorian prefect stood at Trajan's deathbed and announced Hadrian's adoption and succession on 9 August.

properties.name: Pliny the Younger
properties.location_117: Laurentine villa, near Ostia (probable site near modern Castel Fusano)
properties.one_line: Pliny was already dead by this year, his last securely dated letters written from Bithynia-Pontus around 113; his seaside villa near Ostia stood empty of him in 117.

properties.name: Pliny the Younger
properties.location_117: Tuscan villa near Tifernum Tiberinum (modern Città di Castello)
properties.one_line: Pliny's inland estate above the Tiber, described lovingly in his letters, sat unattended in 117, its owner already several years dead.

properties.name: Tacitus
properties.one_line: The 61-year-old former consul and proconsul of Asia was in Rome working on the Annals, having recently finished circulating the Histories.

properties.name: Suetonius
properties.one_line: Suetonius held the posts of director of the imperial libraries and keeper of the archives under Trajan and continued in the post as Hadrian's reign opened, based in Rome rather than at the front.

properties.name: Plutarch
properties.location_117: Chaeronea, Boeotia (holding a lifelong priesthood at nearby Delphi since c. 95)
properties.one_line: The 71-year-old author of the Parallel Lives lived out his final years in his native Chaeronea while still holding his Delphic priesthood.

properties.name: Epictetus
properties.one_line: The formerly enslaved Stoic, about 62 this year, ran his well-known philosophical school at Nicopolis, drawing students from across the Greek and Roman elite.

properties.name: Juvenal
properties.one_line: Juvenal was in Rome finishing Book Two of his Satires, including Satire 6, published around this year.

properties.name: Rufus of Ephesus
properties.one_line: Rufus practiced and wrote medical treatises at Ephesus; ancient sources place his active years under Trajan, though his exact dates remain debated among historians of medicine.

properties.name: Soranus of Ephesus
properties.one_line: The Ephesus-born physician practiced medicine in Rome across the reigns of Trajan and Hadrian, later writing the influential Gynaecology.

properties.name: Arrian
properties.one_line: The roughly 31-year-old Bithynian was studying under Epictetus at Nicopolis around this time, taking the notes that would become the Discourses, decades before his own career as historian and general.

properties.name: Favorinus of Arles
properties.one_line: The Gaulish-born sophist had already built a reputation in Rome and Athens by this year and was moving in the circle that would soon include the new emperor Hadrian.

properties.name: Titus Statilius Crito
properties.location_117: Selinus, Cilicia (probable, attending the dying emperor)
properties.one_line: Trajan's own physician since the Dacian campaigns, known to the Suda as Criton of Heraclea and author of a lost history of those wars called the Getica, was probably still attending the emperor when he died at Selinus.

properties.name: Rabbi Akiva
properties.one_line: In his sixties, Akiva ran his academy at Bnei Brak while the Kitos War burned through nearby Lydda and the wider Jewish diaspora.

properties.name: Rabban Gamaliel II
properties.one_line: The patriarch of the Sanhedrin was caught up in the distress at Lydda during Lusius Quietus's siege of the town, and would die within the year.

properties.name: Ignatius of Antioch
properties.location_117: Rome (site of martyrdom; died c. 108, roughly a decade before this snapshot)
properties.one_line: Ignatius was already dead by this year, condemned to the beasts in Rome's arena around 108 after writing his seven letters on the journey from Antioch.

properties.name: Polycarp of Smyrna
properties.one_line: About 48 years old, Polycarp was already established as bishop of Smyrna, a position he is attested to have held by this year at the latest.

properties.name: Lusius Quietus
properties.one_line: Trajan's Berber cavalry commander, fresh off crushing the Jewish revolt in Mesopotamia, was appointed governor of Judaea in 117 and moved to besiege the rebels holding Lydda.

properties.name: Quintus Marcius Turbo
properties.one_line: Marcius Turbo led a combined land and naval force that crushed the Jewish revolt in Egypt and Cyrenaica through 117, driving the rebel Lukuas out of Alexandria.

properties.name: Lukuas
properties.location_117: Fleeing toward Judaea after the fall of the Cyrenaica-Egypt revolt
properties.one_line: The Jewish rebel leader Cassius Dio calls Andreas, and Eusebius calls a self-styled king, burned Alexandria before being driven out by Marcius Turbo and fleeing east toward Judaea in 117.

properties.name: Chrauttius
properties.role: Cavalry trooper, Ninth Cohort of Batavians
properties.one_line: A Batavian trooper on the northern British frontier who wrote to his old messmate Veldeius, then serving in London, to complain that he never wrote back, pass on greetings to their comrades, and ask him to buy a pair of shears.

properties.name: Veldeius
properties.role: Cavalry trooper, later groom to the provincial governor
properties.one_line: A Batavian trooper who left the frontier for a posting on the governor's staff in London as his personal groom. A scrap of leather cut with his name was found back at Vindolanda, where his friend Chrauttius was still stationed.

properties.name: Octavius
properties.role: Trader in hides, grain and sinew
properties.one_line: A civilian contractor supplying the frontier garrisons who wrote to his associate Candidus about 5,000 measures of grain and 170 hides waiting on a deal, and asked urgently for cash to cover the deposit he had already promised.

properties.name: Masclus
properties.one_line: A cavalry officer who wrote to his prefect asking for the next day's orders and whether all the men should bring the standards back to the crossroads, then added a postscript: his comrades had run out of beer, and would he please send more.

properties.name: Cassius Saecularis
properties.role: Officer in charge of garrison supply
properties.one_line: The man at Vindolanda who received the letters about barley and building timber. Several correspondents wrote to him about getting supplies up to the fort, including an eagle-bearer of the Second Legion writing from South Wales.

properties.name: Severus
properties.one_line: A military clerk who wrote to Candidus, another household's slave, to settle up the cost of goods bought for the Saturnalia and to ask for radishes for the feast. He addressed the enslaved man as brother.
sources: A. Birley et al., 'Slavery on the Northern Frontier: A Stylus Tablet from Vindolanda', Britannia (2024)

properties.name: Candidus
properties.role: Slave of the prefect Flavius Genialis
properties.one_line: An enslaved man who ran the household purchasing for a fort commander on the edge of the empire, buying in supplies for the Saturnalia and haggling over the bill with a legionary clerk who called him brother.
sources: A. Birley et al., 'Slavery on the Northern Frontier: A Stylus Tablet from Vindolanda', Britannia (2024)

properties.name: Cessaucius Nigrinus
properties.one_line: A cavalryman drawing double pay, named as the recipient of a letter from a man called Tullio. His name turns up again on the back of another tablet from the same fort, which puts him at or near Vindolanda.

properties.name: Vittius Adiutor
properties.one_line: The soldier who carried the eagle standard of the Second Legion Augusta, based at the great fortress in South Wales. He wrote north to Vindolanda about supplies, in the tone of one officer to an equal.

properties.name: Tiberius Claudius Maximus
properties.role: Cavalry decurion, veteran of the Dacian Wars
properties.attested: Funerary monument he set up himself, CIL III 14214
properties.one_line: The trooper who ran down the Dacian king Decebalus in 106 CE and carried his severed head to Trajan, and was promoted decurion for it. He retired to Philippi and carved the whole scene onto his own tombstone, where he was still living in 117 CE.
sources: M. Speidel, 'The Captor of Decebalus', Journal of Roman Studies 60 (1970)

properties.name: Marcus Ulpius Phaedimus
properties.one_line: Trajan's 28-year-old cupbearer, chief lictor and keeper of the register of imperial favours. He died at Selinus on 12 August 117, the day after the news of Trajan's own death reached Hadrian. His body waited twelve years for permission to come home to Rome.
sources: Vatican Museums, Galleria Lapidaria, 'Epitaph of a lictor'

properties.name: Claudius Terentianus
properties.role: Sailor of the Alexandrian fleet, later legionary
properties.attested: Letters in the Karanis archive, P.Mich. VIII
properties.one_line: He enlisted in the Alexandrian fleet around 110 CE and transferred into the Twenty-Second Legion during the Jewish revolt of 115-117. His letters home to his father survive because the family kept them in a niche under the stairs.

properties.name: Claudius Tiberianus
properties.attested: Letters in the Karanis archive, P.Mich. VIII
properties.one_line: A discharged army courier settled in a Fayum village, receiving letters from his son Terentianus in the fleet. Excavators found the whole family correspondence stuffed into a niche beneath his staircase, exactly where he left it.

properties.name: Gaius Julius Apollinarius
properties.one_line: A soldier posted to the new province of Arabia who wrote home asking his father to pull strings and get him a desk job as a company clerk, rather than the stone-cutting and quarry work the rest of the legion was doing.

properties.name: Apion (Antonius Maximus)
properties.one_line: An Egyptian villager who crossed the sea to join the fleet and wrote home to his father the moment he landed: the voyage was safe, the emperor's travel money had come through, and he had a Roman name now.

properties.name: Babatha
properties.location_117: Maoza, Arabia Petraea (near modern Ghor es-Safi, Jordan)
properties.one_line: A Jewish woman farming date palms on the south shore of the Dead Sea, who kept every deed, lawsuit and marriage contract of her life in a leather purse. She hid it in a cave during the revolt of 132 and never came back for it.

properties.name: Shimon son of Menahem
properties.location_117: Maoza, Arabia Petraea (near modern Ghor es-Safi, Jordan)
properties.attested: Deed of 99 CE and later documents in the Babatha archive
properties.one_line: Babatha's father, who bought a date-palm orchard from the Nabataean governor Archelaus in 99 CE and later signed it over to his daughter. He was still alive in 117 CE and dead by 124.

properties.name: Jesus son of Jesus
properties.role: Villager of Maoza, Babatha's first husband
properties.location_117: Maoza, Arabia Petraea (near modern Ghor es-Safi, Jordan)
properties.one_line: Babatha's first husband and the father of her only son. He was alive at the 117 CE snapshot and dead before 124, leaving her to fight the Petra town council for years over the boy's guardianship money.

properties.name: Salome Komaise
properties.location_117: Maoza, Arabia Petraea (near modern Ghor es-Safi, Jordan)
properties.attested: Personal archive, XHev/Se papyri, c. 125-131 CE
properties.one_line: A second woman of the same Dead Sea village who hid a second bundle of legal papers in the same cave. Her documents cover a tax registration, a property settlement and her own marriage certificate.
sources: H. Cotton, 'The Archive of Salome Komaise Daughter of Levi'

properties.name: Judah Khthousion
properties.one_line: An En-Gedi man with three date orchards who became Babatha's second husband and legal guardian. He was already married to Miriam when he married her, and his death left the two women suing each other over his estate.

properties.name: Miriam daughter of Beianus
properties.one_line: Judah Khthousion's first wife, who went on sharing a husband with Babatha and then went to court against her over what he left behind. Her brother Jonathan appears in the same papers.

properties.name: Shelamzion daughter of Judah
properties.location_117: Maoza, Arabia Petraea (near modern Ghor es-Safi, Jordan)
properties.one_line: Judah Khthousion's daughter, whose Greek marriage contract of 128 CE survives in full, dowry and all. She was a child in the household at the 117 CE snapshot.

properties.name: Judah Cimber
properties.one_line: Son of Ananias son of Somalas, of En-Gedi but living at Maoza. He married Shelamzion in 128 CE under a contract that spells out her dowry and his obligations in Greek legal formula.

properties.name: Abdoobdas son of Illouthas
properties.role: Guardian appointed by the council of Petra
properties.one_line: A Nabataean named by the Petra town council as guardian of Babatha's orphaned son, on an allowance she thought insulting. She took the council to court over the amount and the file survives.
sources: H. Cotton, 'The Guardianship of Jesus Son of Babatha', JRS

properties.name: John son of Eglas
properties.role: Guardian appointed by the council of Petra
properties.one_line: The Jewish half of the pair of guardians the Petra council put over Babatha's son. He and his Nabataean colleague between them paid the boy a monthly allowance his mother took them to court to increase.
sources: H. Cotton, 'The Guardianship of Jesus Son of Babatha', JRS
